real_world_anchor.primary: A steady whistled note on a phone's sound-display app. A whistle is the everyday sound closest to a single sine wave — no other common sound is this close to one pure oscillation. It also sets up the S4/S5 reinforcement exactly: a louder whistle draws a taller wave (the a state), a higher-pitched whistle draws a narrower one (the b state). Delivered verbatim in STATE_1's narration: 'Whistle a steady note at a phone — its display shows this same wave shape.'

b.name: horizontal stretch factor (compresses the input before sin acts)

xdraw.name: S1 draw-in edge — the parent's growing right boundary

hg.name: S3 guess-curve offset (the WRONG sweep, never the real h)

constraints: the full transform y = a*sin(b*(x-h)) + k is defined for every real x and every (a,b,h,k) in their authored ranges, with zero excluded points — the slider floor b >= 0.5 everywhere keeps b(x-h) from degenerating into a constant, structurally, not by convention

the drawn interval is x in [-6.5, 6.5] in S2-S8 (S1 draws the same interval progressively); the underlying relation is defined on all of R — no caption, chip or narration string may claim the curve stops existing at the frame edge

range of the drawn transform = [k - |a|, k + |a|], contained in [-4, 4] for every (a,k) in the full explore control product (worst case |a|+|k| = 3.5, 12.5% headroom) — D4 break-on-range-exit is never exercised by this concept
P' = (pi/2/b + h, a + k) is the image of the parent's peak P = (pi/2, 1) under the full transform, recomputed fresh every frame from a, b, h, k — never accumulated, never interpolated between frames

the S5 width bracket spans [0, 2*pi/b] in data x at fixed y = -1.6; at S5's own slider floor b = 1 this is 6.283 data units against a 13-unit-wide frame, an 0.217-unit margin — S5's b-range is deliberately narrower than S8's for exactly this reason

every choreographed hold and every eye_capture_ms pin lands on a value exactly representable at 1 decimal place (the slider-caption display grid) — enforced by choosing all four parameters' step = 0.5, uniformly, a mathematics_author decision extending the architect's a/h/k step to b

tts_sentences.text_en: Parent curve — the base graph.
This is the sine curve — the height of a circling point, laid out flat.
Whistle a steady note at a phone — its display shows this same wave shape.

STATE_2.title: Add k: The Curve Slides Up

tts_sentences.text_en: The dim ghost is the parent, sin x, held still.
The bright copy is sin x plus k: as k rises from zero, the copy slides straight up by k.
P′ rises with it — the peak's image.

STATE_3.title: Subtract h Inside: It Slides Right

misconception_watch.belief: y = f(x − h) with h > 0 shifts the graph LEFT — minus means left
misconception_watch.visual_counter: the frozen guess curve held beside the real copy moving the other way (6800–11000 ms — both on screen, travelling apart, for 4.2 s)
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: x − h asks for a larger x to give the old value — the curve moves right.

tts_sentences.text_en: The dashed guess curve slides left, then freezes — the wrong direction.
The real copy slides right instead: x minus h equals the old value only when x is larger.
Both sit apart on screen until the guess fades.

STATE_4.title: Multiply by a: Flipped, Then Twice as Tall

tts_sentences.text_en: Outside multiplication differs from outside addition: a scales every height, not the position.
As a runs from one to negative two, the copy shrinks, flips, grows twice as tall upside down.
P′, the peak's image, travels straight down.

STATE_5.title: Multiply x by b: Squeezed Narrower

misconception_watch.belief: b = 2 stretches the graph wider — bigger number, bigger graph
misconception_watch.visual_counter: the stepping bracket against the fixed ghost period
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: b multiplies x before sin acts — the width divides by b.

tts_sentences.text_en: Bigger b does not mean a wider curve — it means narrower.
As b increases from one to three in counted steps, the width bracket shrinks: two pi over b.
b multiplies x before sine acts, so the width divides by b.

STATE_6.title: Outside Acts on y, Inside Acts on x

scene_composition.text: outside — acts on y, as written
inside — acts on x, the opposite way (÷ b, + h)

tts_sentences.text_en: Two outside numbers move first: k lifts the curve, then a stretches it — both act on y, as written (× a, + k).
Two inside numbers follow: h shifts the curve right, b squeezes it narrower — both act on x, the opposite way.

scene_composition.equation:
f(x) → a·f(b(x − h)) + k
(x₀, y₀) → (x₀/b + h, a·y₀ + k)

tts_sentences.text_en: Write f for whatever curve you started with — here it was sine.
One point moves in four hops: divide its x by b, then add h; multiply its y by a, then add k.
Order matters — divide first, then add.

aha_moment.statement: Outside numbers move y the way they say; inside numbers move x the opposite way.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: the k-then-a pair completes before the 'outside acts on y' chip; the h-then-b pair completes before the 'inside acts on x' chip

assessment.mastery_definition: A student has mastered this concept when they can name the midline after an outside addition, the shift direction after an inside subtraction, the amplitude and orientation after an outside multiplication including a sign flip, the period after an inside multiplication, write the equation for a curve moved both sideways and vertically, and map one point through the full transform in the correct divide-then-add order.

questions.stem: The curve y = sin x + 2 is graphed. What straight line is the curve's midline?

distractor_misconceptions.B: treats +2 as changing only the curve's steepness, leaving the midline at the parent's own y = 0
distractor_misconceptions.C: reads the vertical shift number as a horizontal line instead of a vertical one
distractor_misconceptions.D: flips the sign of k, sliding the midline down instead of up

questions.tested_idea: adding k outside the function slides the midline vertically by exactly k

questions.stem: The curve y = sin(x − 1.5) is graphed. Compared with y = sin x, the curve has moved

distractor_misconceptions.A: reads the minus sign inside the bracket as a leftward move
distractor_misconceptions.C: mistakes the inside subtraction for an outside vertical shift
distractor_misconceptions.D: mistakes the inside subtraction for a downward vertical shift with the wrong sign

questions.tested_idea: x minus h inside the function slides the curve RIGHT by h, the opposite of the naive minus-means-left reading

questions.stem: The curve y = −2 sin x is graphed. Its amplitude and orientation compared with y = sin x are

distractor_misconceptions.B: reports the amplitude as the signed coefficient −2 instead of its magnitude
distractor_misconceptions.C: captures the height doubling but misses that a negative a flips the curve
distractor_misconceptions.D: confuses multiplying by 2 with dividing by 2, shrinking instead of stretching

questions.tested_idea: a outside the function scales every height by |a|, and a negative a flips the curve

questions.stem: What is the period of y = sin 4x?

distractor_misconceptions.A: multiplies the parent's period 2π by 4 instead of dividing by it
distractor_misconceptions.B: multiplies the parent's period 2π by 2 instead of dividing by 4
distractor_misconceptions.D: keeps the parent's own period unchanged, missing that b squeezes it

questions.tested_idea: b inside the function divides the period by b — bigger b means a narrower, not wider, curve

questions.stem: Which equation describes the curve y = sin x moved 3 units right and 1 unit up?

distractor_misconceptions.B: moves the curve right by writing +3 inside the bracket instead of −3
distractor_misconceptions.C: moves the curve down by keeping the minus sign in front of the outside 1
distractor_misconceptions.D: swaps which number is the inside shift and which is the outside shift

questions.tested_idea: outside numbers act on y the way they say; inside numbers act on x the opposite way

questions.stem: Under y = 2 sin(2(x − 1)) + 1, the parent's peak at (π/2, 1) lands at

distractor_misconceptions.B: skips dividing the x-coordinate by b before adding h
distractor_misconceptions.C: multiplies the x-coordinate by b instead of dividing by it
distractor_misconceptions.D: subtracts h instead of adding it after dividing by b

questions.tested_idea: a point maps by dividing x by b THEN adding h; multiplying y by a THEN adding k — order matters
